en: The Scripture on the Ritual for the Accomplishment of the Great Vidyā of the Bodhisattva Tārā from the Yoga Mahātantra of the Vidyādharapiṭaka, Spoken by the Buddha. Fascicle One.
Part One: The Section on the Accomplishment of the Great Vidyā. Part One.

Nāgārjuna Bodhisattva extracted this from the Vidyādharapiṭaka. Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Imperial Bestower of the Title Chao San Dafu, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, Great Master Mingjiao, the Subject Faxian, by Imperial Decree. At that time, the World-Honored One said:
Regarding this Great Yoga Teaching of the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana:
if there is a son of good family who desires to practice the various methods for attaining accomplishments (siddhi), [he should do so as follows].
One should single-mindedly and diligently practice this Great Vidyā-dhāraṇī method of the Bodhisattva Kuntī within this teaching; then,
whatever one seeks or aspires for will be accomplished without exception.
If there is a practitioner who wishes to achieve the most supreme and excellent accomplishment,
they should first go to the edge of a great ocean shore.
Recite the root vidyā-mantra of the Bodhisattva Cunda;
once you have completed six lakṣas of constructing sand stupas,
whatever you seek will certainly be accomplished.
Furthermore, if one wishes to seek a vision of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva,
or Tārā Bodhisattva, or Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva, and so forth,
one should practice as previously described.
These bodhisattvas will certainly manifest their forms to comfort the practitioner and fulfill their aspirations,
even performing rites such as those for winning affection and so forth.
Some seek various kinds of sacred medicines;
some seek the rank of an Asura king;
and some seek the rank of a Vidyādhara.
Such matters will certainly be accomplished.
If one practices with long-term cultivation, focused concentration,
and without regression, even the stage of a Bodhisattva may be attained.
Furthermore, if a practitioner recites a *mahāvidyā* ten million times before a Buddha stūpa or at a site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*),
upon completing the count of recitations, they shall attain the state of an Arhat.
By manifesting his body and speech, he attains great benefit.
Thereafter, he travels together with the Arhats and shares their majestic power.
Furthermore, the practitioner proceeds to the summit of Mount Vimalasvabhāva.
Constantly eating from his alms bowl before a Buddhist stūpa,
he recited the Great Mantra one koṭi times.
Once the number of recitations was complete,
One beholds the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi.
The Bodhisattva personally leads the practitioner into the auspicious gate and says to them: "Enter this gate."
Free from all demonic obstacles, their aspirations will be fulfilled;
liberated from all fears, they shall experience great bliss and, in the future, behold Maitreya.
Upon hearing the exposition of the sublime Dharma, one realizes the stages of a bodhisattva, or even attains the rank of an *avaivartika* bodhisattva.
Furthermore, the practitioner may go to the summit of Mount Vipula.
Always maintaining complete purity while eating from one’s alms bowl,
one should prepare incense, flowers, lamps, and ointments according to one's means before an image containing relics, and perform offerings.
Recite the great mantra three hundred thousand times.
Once the count is complete,
the practitioner should separately prepare extensive offerings.
The practitioner shall redouble their purity and observe the fast.
On the fifteenth day, they shall recite the mantra without ceasing throughout the entire day and night;
Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva will then certainly manifest his form to welcome and guide the practitioner.
From his own palace, he went to the Auspicious Gate and caused the practitioner to enter it,
whereby the practitioner’s lifespan was extended to equal that of the sun and moon.
Furthermore, the practitioner went to the place of the Buddha-stūpa with its three jeweled stairways.
Constantly carrying his alms bowl, he circumambulated the Buddha’s stūpa to the right.
Having recited the Great Mantra one koṭi times,
once the count was complete—
One shall obtain the vision of Ajita and Hārītī, through whom all that is sought is fulfilled as desired.
This Hārītī will lead the practitioner to her own palace and bestow various types of sacred medicines.
The Invincible One manifests his form to teach the Dharma to the practitioner so that they may realize the path to enlightenment and bestow upon them the sacred medicine;
he transforms the practitioner’s body so that it possesses extraordinary marks.
Furthermore, one shall attain the guidance and realization of the path of all bodhisattvas,
up until swiftly sitting at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
This is the Great Vidyā-mantra of Cundā.
This has been proclaimed by all the Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas alike;
it brings great benefit to sentient beings,
even unto the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Furthermore, if there are sentient beings who have committed great evil deeds and lack the seeds of goodness,
there is no means by which the bodhicitta can arise within them.
Such a person, who has never before attained the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma),
suddenly encounters a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) who recites this great vidyā-mantra so that it passes once through their faculty of hearing.
Even for one whose heavy sins have diminished their virtuous seeds, [the result] will arise;
how much more so for a practitioner who constantly recites with focused diligence?
Such a person who seeks accomplishment will certainly attain it.
2. Section on the Accomplishment of Contemplative Wisdom (Vipaśyanā-jñāna-siddhi-bhāga), Part One of Two.
Furthermore, if a practitioner wishes to cultivate the various methods of accomplishment (*siddhi*), [they should proceed as follows].
First, one must cultivate contemplative wisdom;
once all mudrās and their characteristics have been mastered with precision so that no error remains, only then may one seek the various siddhis.
If one seeks siddhi within the dharma of the Bodhisattva Kuntā,
one should first visualize the fundamental, subtle wheel of syllables of the Bodhisattva Kuntā as being established within one's own body.
That is to say: visualize the syllable Oṃ placed upon the head;
visualize the syllable Va placed upon the two eyes;
visualize the syllable Lī placed upon the neck.
Visualize the character *tsu* (卒) and place it upon the two arms;
again, visualize the character *lei* (隸) and place it upon the heart;
visualize the character *zun* (尊) and place it within the navel.
One visualizes the syllable *ṇe* and places it upon the two thighs;
one visualizes the syllable *svā* and places it upon the two calves.
The practitioner thus contemplates these subtle and wondrous syllabic forms of the root mantra of Bhadraśrī.
Once each and every part of one's own body has been clearly visualized,
all sinful karma committed in previous lives will be entirely extinguished.
The sought-after siddhi will certainly be accomplished.
Whether performing rites for pacification, enrichment, subjugation, or magnetizing,
the respective vidyās to be recited differ for each.
The great mantra recited for the rite of pacifying calamities is:
Oṃ cale cule cuṇḍe svāhā. The great mantra recited for the rite of increasing prosperity is: [Oṃ jvalini jvalini prajvalini hūṃ phaṭ svāhā].
Oṃ cale cule cuṇḍe vaśam ānaya svāhā. This is the great vidyā-mantra for performing the rite of subjugation (vaśīkaraṇa).
Oṃ cale cule cuṇḍe namas. This is the great vidyā-mantra for performing the rite of subduing (damana).
Oṃ cale cule cuṇḍe jaḥ hīḥ hūṃ phaṭ. If one performs the four aforementioned rites, it is essential to invoke the principal deity and the assembly of worthy sages.
When the ritual procedure is completed, perform the dismissal.
The Great Mantra for summoning is:
Oṃ cale cule cuṇḍe hili. The Great Mantra for dismissal is: [as follows].
Oṃ cale cule cuṇḍe hūṃ. Furthermore, when the practitioner constructs the maṇḍala and wishes to invite the principal deity and summon the noble beings within the altar, [he should recite this].
First, recite the Vajra Great Mantra *Cili Cili* to perform purification. The mantra is:
Oṃ cili cili vajra hūṃ phaṭ. Having performed the purification by reciting this mantra, [proceed].
The practitioner visualizes the deity Kuan-yin (Avalokiteśvara) descending from the Akaniṣṭha Heaven and entering the maṇḍala.
Furthermore, one should visualize within the maṇḍala a lion throne,
universally adorned with various lotuses; then,
one should form the mudrā for offering the seat and recite the mantra for offering the seat.
Having requested the Bodhisattva to be seated,
one should immediately bind the fundamental mudrā of the Bodhisattva and recite the fundamental vidyā-mantra to make offerings to the Bodhisattva.
The practitioner then says, "Welcome, O Bodhisattva," and offers argha water and other offerings;
thereafter, he performs the ritual and engages in recitation.
Furthermore, the practitioner, having constructed the maṇḍala according to the ritual and performed the boundary-binding and purification rites,
stands before the maṇḍala.
Sitting upright with right mindfulness, perform the visualization:
imagine the fundamental, subtle wheel of syllables before you,
and place them upon the various parts of the body.
First, visualize all Tathāgatas upon the crown of one’s head.
While forming this visualization, employ the binding of the samaya-mudrā.
Next, visualize the syllable *vaṃ* at both eyes.
One should employ the Buddha-eye mudrā.
Furthermore, one should visualize this syllable transforming into a Wheel-turning King (Cakravartin) of great power.
Next, one should visualize the syllable *ḷe* as black in color at the nape of the neck, using the conch-shell mudrā (*śaṅkha-mudrā*).
He immediately transforms into the Great Fierce Wrathful King Acala,
holding a sword and a noose in his hands.
Next, visualize the syllable *tsuṭ* appearing upon his heart.
He immediately transforms into the body of a Buddha, red in color and possessing four arms.
Two hands are joined in the gesture of prostration at the crown of the head;
two hands form the *dharmacakra-mudrā* (teaching seal) in the manner of subduing all māras.
Again, visualize the syllable *LĪ* appearing on both arms;
one should employ the *Svastika* mudrā.
On one arm, it transforms into the Bodhisattva Amoghapāśa.
The face has three eyes.
One arm transforms above into the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara,
whose body is yellow in color.
Next, visualize the syllable *Bhṛṅ* appearing at the navel wheel;
one should employ the fundamental mudrā of Bhṛṅgin to transform [oneself] into the deity, the Bodhisattva Bhṛṅgin.
If one visualizes the eighteen-armed body as white,
or the six-armed body as yellow, or the four-armed body as red.
Once the visualized signs have appeared before him as he contemplates them,
he should imagine that this Bodhisattva is able to bring great benefit to the triple world.
Next, he should imagine the syllable *ṇi* appearing on his two thighs.
By employing the auspicious mudrā,
one immediately transforms into a Buddha or a Bodhisattva,
capable of accomplishing all tasks.
Next, visualize the syllable *Sva* appearing on both calves.
Then, using the conch seal and the sword seal,
transform the upper part of the left calf into *Gṛhāṇa*.
On the right calf, it transforms into the syllable Jñāṃ.
Next, visualize the syllable Ha appearing on both feet.
Employ the lotus mudrā.
He immediately transforms into the Vajranakhī Vidyārājñī,
holding a noose in her hand.
Next, one employs the mudrā and the great mantra of the Bodhisattva Buddhalocanā.
One performs the empowerment of the five places with the mantra:
Oṃ ruru-sapara jvala tiṣṭha siddhalocani sarvārthasādhani svāhā. Furthermore, the practitioner, having cultivated the wisdom of contemplation, [proceeds].
Rising from one's seat, perform the mudrā of joining the palms at the crown of the head and recite the great mantra:
*Namo sabhdatānām* (1) *samyaksaṃbuddhakūṭānām* (2) *namo jvale* (3) *jvalane* (4). By the power of this great mantra, all māras are subdued.
There shall be no Māras or celestial Māras who dare to oppose him.
Next, one employs the seal of dismissal to dispatch all Māras,
ensuring that the practitioner encounters no obstacles.
The mudrā for dispatching māras:
extend and shake the left hand to create the gesture of expulsion;
the right hand forms the samādhi-vajra gesture.
Resting on the right side of the waist,
he treads upon the ground with his left foot in a wrathful manner.
He recites the great mantra as follows:
Namo (1) ājñe (2) jūḷe (3) svanī (4) hana (5) naha (6) matha (7) vicitra-sayūṣarāyate (8) hūṃ phaṭ (9). Next, perform the mudrā for binding the boundary.
With both hands in the space above, below, and in the ten directions,
rotate them like the wind to form the mudrā;
then recite the great mantra as follows:
Oṃ cale cule cuṇḍe daka daka jvala jvala sarva-niśu-manda manda hūṃ. This mantra may be used for the purpose of binding the boundary (sīmā-bandha) in all places.
Next, using the Sarvasiddhi-vidyā,
consecrate the fragrant unguents and pure water;
having entered the maṇḍala, sprinkle them for purification.
Then, form the *kūṭāgāra-mudrā*:
with both hands held palms up and interlaced, slightly bent,
extend the two index fingers and the two thumbs.
Form the mudrā by placing it alongside the side of the index finger.
When binding this mudrā,
visualize a most supreme and exquisite palace and pavilion.
Once it has been brought before one,
one further visualizes that subtle and wondrous syllables transform into various exquisite lotus flowers, adorning the lion throne.
When this visualization is accomplished:
He then recited the mantra for invocation to summon the principal deity and the assembly of worthy sages,
who entered and took their seats within.
Accordingly, one should establish the deity of one's own family as the central seat;
if Kuntā is taken as the deity of one's own family,
then Kuntā herself is established as the central seat.
One should then visualize the Bodhisattva Tārā with eighteen arms;
her body is white like the color of the autumn moon,
and she wears white garments and various ornaments.
He wears bracelets made of cat's-eye gemstone,
and each of his ten fingers is adorned with rings;
his face has three eyes.
The two upper hands on both sides form the gesture of teaching the Dharma (*dharmacakra-mudrā*).
The second right hand forms the gesture of granting fearlessness (*abhaya-mudrā*),
and the third right hand holds a sword.
The fourth hand holds a real bell;
the fifth hand holds a vijapura fruit;
the sixth hand holds a battle-axe.
The seventh hand holds a hook;
the eighth hand grasps a vajra;
the ninth hand holds a rosary.
In his second left hand he holds a wish-fulfilling jewel banner;
in his third hand he holds a lotus flower;
and in his fourth hand he holds a khaṭvāṅga staff.
The fifth hand holds a lasso;
the sixth hand holds a wheel;
the seventh hand holds a conch shell.
The eighth hand holds an *udakamaṇi* (vase of excellence).
The ninth hand holds the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
To the right, one should place the Bodhisattva Buddhalocanā and the assembly of worthy sages (*ārya*).
On the left side, one should install Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva and Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva,
along with all other bodhisattvas and the assembly of worthy sages,
arranging them as desired.
Furthermore, using the *vidyā* of Sarvasiddhi and the *vidyā* of the Bodhisattva Locanā,
consecrate the argha water, incense, and flowers;
then burn the incense and offer it to the principal deity and the assembly of worthy sages.
He then addressed them, saying:
"O Bodhisattvas and all worthy sages, by my faith and through the power of this samādhi,
I offer these argha, incense, flowers, and other such items."
I pray that you, out of compassion, will accept my offerings.
As for the argha water:
if it is used for the rite of pacification (śāntika), one should prepare it by mixing milk with barley.
If performing a rite of enrichment (*puṣṭi*), add sesame seeds;
if performing a rite of subjugation (*abhicāra*), add blood and buckwheat together.
There are also differences in the *argha* water used and the vessels for holding the *argha*.
Then he spoke of the mudrā for summoning: using the bathing mudrā, one modifies it by placing the two thumbs alongside the sides of the index fingers;
when formed in this manner, it constitutes the hook mudrā.

The mantra for summoning the Great Radiance (*mahāprabhā*) is as follows: *Namaḥ samyak-sambuddha-koṭīnām | Āhvaya-āgavatī | Iṣṭa-nirvātadiṣṭite | Oṃ cale cule cuṇḍe | Cūṃ cūṃ svāhā*. Having recited this mantra, [one should proceed].
When reciting the mantra for offering the seat, say:
*Oṃ kamala svāhā*. Next, explain the sword mudrā;
this is also the mudrā of the Vidyārāja Acala.
Form a fist with the left hand using the thumb, ring finger, and little finger;
extend the index and middle fingers.
With the right hand, [extend] the index and middle fingers.
Insert [the thumb] into the left fist;
the remaining fingers likewise form a fist to constitute the mudrā.
The Great Mantra of Acala is as follows:
Namo samantavajrāṇām | Oṃ aśvakaghaṃ jaṃ ṣaṭya hūṃ phaṭ | Then he spoke the Samaya-mudrā.
Press the thumb of the right hand against the small fingernail;
with the remaining fingers arranged in the form of a vajra, form the mudrā.
Having bound this mudrā, recite the samaya vidyā-mantra as follows:
Oṃ śaṅkari samaye svāhā. Second, the offering of the arghya mudrā:
perform the bathing mudrā, with the only modification being that the thumbs are extended.
Form the mudrā by placing the tips of the index fingers together in the gesture of *añjali*.
The great mantra is: Oṃ jale jvale jvāle arghapādyaiḥ pratīccha svāhā. Having offered the *argha* water, [proceed].
The practitioner joins the palms and speaks these words:
"O Great Bodhisattva, I pray that you will compassionately accept this offering.
The practitioner then again employs the Vajrakīla mudrā.
To bind the boundary and expel māras,
one uses the vajra as the boundary.
The boundary thus established functions according to the ritual procedure.
Alternatively, when performing a great rite of malevolent dharma,
one should form this mudrā by making the index finger of the right hand like a hook and placing the thumb like a needle facing downward.
This is the Great Mantra of the Kīla-mudrā:
Oṃ bhuḍini kīlaya svāhā. [Next] is the Binding Vajra-realm Mudrā.
Without altering the previous mudrā, form the hook with the index finger of the right hand;
with the index finger of the left hand held straight up,
form the seal and rotate it in the space before you.
The mantra for binding the Vajradhātu is: Oṃ bhuḥ ṭiṇṭiṇi prākāraya svāhā. Next, bind the Vajrāñjali mudrā.
Without altering the previous mudrā, interlace the two index fingers and the two middle fingers;
move them back and forth above the head to form the seal.
The Great Mantra is as follows:
Oṃ bhaṭṭārakārya-hanajara svāhā. Second, bind the root mudrā and recite the root mantra three times.
Next, bind the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) and recite the Great Mantra seven times.
Next, bind the Trident Seal (triśūlamudrā):
form fists with both hands.
Extend the index, middle, and ring fingers of each hand like a trident to form the mudrā.
The Great Mantra is:
Oṃ Bhagavati Svāhā. Next, bind the mudrā of the pestle (mudgara).
Form fists with both hands and interlace the two thumbs to form the mudrā.
The great mantra is as follows:
Oṃ cale hūṃ. Next, perform the banner mudrā:
with the index and middle fingers of the left hand, extend each upright and move them to form the seal.
The Great Illumination says:
Oṃ. Next, for the Honored One, perform the Banner Seal (dhvaja-mudrā):
form a fist with the right hand.
Form the mudrā by extending the index and middle fingers straight upward.
The Great Illumination mantra is: Oṃ. Next, recite the heart-mantra of Acala.
And with the heart-mantra of Vajranakhā,
one consecrates incense, flowers, and so forth as pure offerings.
The heart-mantra of Acala is as follows:
Oṃ āḥ hūṃ phaṭ. Recite this second time. Next, recite the heart-mantra of Vajranakhā:
Oṃ jina-jik. Next, form the mudrā of the scented unguent (gandha).
With the thumb of the right hand,
pinch the tip of the index finger and extend the remaining fingers.
Form this mudrā and recite the mantra to empower the incense,
which is then offered to the principal deity and the assembly of worthy sages.
The great mantra is as follows:
Oṃ le svāhā. Next, form the flower mudrā;
without changing the previous mudrā, recite the great mantra:
Oṃ bhuje svāhā. Next, form the incense mudrā.
Form the mudrā by pressing the tip of the middle finger with the thumb of the right hand,
and recite the great mantra as follows:
Oṃ le svāhā. Next, form the mudrā of manifestation:
with the left hand, join the thumb and the index finger to form the seal.
Then, recite the mantra for offering food:
*Oṃ bhadre svāhā*. Next, form the mudrā for offering lamps using the thumb of the right hand.
Form the mudrā by joining the first joints of the middle fingers.
The Great Mantra is:
Oṃ de svāhā. As previously described, these and other offering implements are presented to the Buddhas and the assembly of noble ones.
Even down to food, drink, incense, flowers, and so forth—
all mudrās and great mantras (mahāvidyā) are to be arranged according to the sequential order of their respective families.
If one performs rites such as the *śāntika* (pacification), one first uses scented unguents and so forth,
and then forms the mudrās for offering and worship;
one may then perform visualizations either internally or externally.
Offer all these offerings to the noble ones and sages.
Next, bind the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā):
form fists with both hands.
Visualize this within the mind.
Form the mudrā with the letter A appearing within each of the two palms.
Offer this mudrā to all the worthy sages and holy ones.
Next, form the Lotus Mudrā:
join the two hands together;
extend the eight fingers so they are slightly separated from one another like the appearance of a lotus, and bend the two thumbs into the palms to complete the mudrā.
Having bound this mudrā, offer it to the various worthy sages with the Great Illumination Mantra:
Oṃ cale cule cuṇḍe svāhā śrī-lokajyeṣṭhe māṣataḥ. Then, bind the root mudrā once more.
Form the añjali with both hands;
extend the two thumbs and insert them into the palms to form the mudrā.
The root mantra is as follows:
Oṃ bhuṭṭārya asphālana | Oṃ juti sapūra | Apasphāraṇa | Oṃ bhuha nara rañja. [Perform] the seal of the eight-spoked wheel.
With both hands turned palm-to-palm,
extend and splay the ten fingers;
press the back of the left hand with the right hand to form the seal.
Moving it above the crown of the head, recite the great mantra:
Oṃ bhagavan prasphura jvala. Then, bind the pāśa-mudrā (noose seal).
Join the two hands together;
form the seal by interlocking the two ring fingers like a lock.
Recite the great mantra as follows:
Oṃ bhaḥ hūṃ phaṭ. Next, form the hook seal (*ākarṣaṇamudrā*):
with the left hand, bend the thumb, ring finger, little finger, and index finger into the shape of a hook to form the seal.
Recite the Great Mantra:
Oṃ cale cule cuḍe svāhā. Then, perform the seal for the extensive offering of worship.
Join the two hands in *añjali*;
bend the third joints of all ten fingers so that they do not touch one another to form the mudrā.
Place it upon the crown of the head.
When the practitioner forms this mudrā,
they should give rise to an inconceivable mind.
With a mind free from the notion of "mine" and a mind devoid of grasping or rejecting,
one further visualizes all the exquisite incense, flowers, and rare jewels of the world,
even including the jewel mountains and the treasures within the great oceans.
All things appear before them;
they are used to make offerings to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
This merit is dedicated and bestowed upon the Tathatā Dharmadhātu.
Furthermore, one should direct the mind so that the merit obtained from such offerings as I have made is successively transformed into immeasurable offerings,
which are then presented to all the Tathāgatas of the ten directions.
And to the great assembly of Bodhisattvas:
may the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas not forsake their great compassion, but graciously accept these offerings.
The mantra for the vast and universal offering is as follows: [Mantra]

*Namo sarvatathāgatebhyo viśvamukhebhyaḥ | Sarvathā khaṃ samudragate sphara hīṃ gaganakaṃ svāhā.* The First Fascicle of the *Buddhabhāṣita-vidyottama-jñāna-siddhi-kalpa-yoga-mahātantra* The Second Fascicle of the *Buddhabhāṣita-vidyottama-jñāna-siddhi-kalpa-yoga-mahātantra*
The Second Part of the Section on the Accomplishment of Contemplative Wisdom.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Dharma Xian, Imperial Censor of the Court, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, and Great Master of Illuminating Teaching, Prince Nāgārjuna, from the *Vidyādharapiṭaka*. By Imperial Decree. Furthermore, [this section] praises the Triple Gem and all the worthy sages.
In praise of the Buddha:
My Buddha, through great compassion, tames all sentient beings and becomes an ocean of merit and virtue; therefore, I praise and pay homage to him.
Praise of the Dharma:
The sublime principle of True Suchness Can destroy all evil realms;
It benefits sentient beings and abides in tranquility— Therefore, I praise and pay homage to it.
In praise of the Saṅgha:
Firmly maintaining the practice of the precepts, Realizing and entering the gates of liberation,
Abiding in the realm of supreme merit— Therefore, I offer praise and prostration.
Praise to the Bodhisattva Cunda and all the worthy sages: Oṃ lakṣmīlakṣaṇadevi sarvalakṣaṇamaṇidhāne praṇamya.
Galam gala ya śaraṇa jagata pṛyā svāmaya somanasan devaya varaha varana pṛyā padma sa.
Namaḥ padmamukhe vimale viśvanākṣa kumārīkaste tapasā uṇāryakṣamāprabhāvajña.
Nirjaraṇi smara mahāmitu-gavalśani amitā-mṛta-vāsa a-ra-a-mara-duruvaḥ si.
dhāsiddhāya āli svapratyāhataṃ jñeti niryā daśaparāmiprāptā daśabhūmiṣu saṃkhye.
Dvaya-saṃyoga-bahula-tīrthaka-janany-ātmike amṛta-prasādani jagan-nikṣepa-kṣame. (1)
*Prāṅkṛpānīta-gajadri-sarvabuddhānām savidricchājinuras-tāṇabhūtārjaga.*

place the thumb in the palm to form the mudrā.
Next is the Crown Mudrā:
form a seal by joining the middle finger, held like a needle, with the right thumb.
If this mudrā is used together with the Great Mantra of the Armor,
it is also called the Armor Mudrā.
Next is the fundamental mudrā of Tārā.
First, move the thumbs of both hands;
then, join the palms of both hands and form the seal by inserting the right thumb into the hollow of the palm.
Rest it upon the heart.
Next is the Flower Seal:
form fists with both hands.
Again, hold both hands upright like needles;
join the tips of the index fingers with the thumbs to form the seal.
Next is the Great Seal.
Place the two hands side by side with the fingers not touching.
Place the thumbs on the third joints of the little fingers.
Then, form a firm fist to complete the mudrā.
Place this mudrā upon one’s own heart and recite the Great Mantra seven times; it can accomplish all dharmas.
Next is the second mudrā.
Then, using the previous mudrā, raise the two thumbs and extend the remaining fingers so that they do not touch one another;
this forms the third mudrā.
For the previous seal, use the index fingers;
place them each upon the third joint of the middle fingers to form the seal.
For the fourth seal, extend both index fingers.
Again, bend the middle joints of each finger respectively.
Then place the middle fingers and ring fingers upon the thumbs.
Finally, place the middle fingers and ring fingers at the middle joints to form the seal.
Next is the seal of the Sūtra:
with the thumbs of both the left and right hands,
pinch the respective small fingernails.
Again, place the right hand upon the left hand to form the seal.
Next is the conch seal (*śaṅkhamudrā*):
join the tips of the index fingers and middle fingers of both hands and extend them straight out.
Grasp the thumb nail with the little finger;
this forms the seal of firmness.
Next is the Seal of Stability.
First, sit in the full lotus posture and extend both hands;
place the right hand over the left,
with the two thumbs touching at their nails.
Place it at ease below the navel to form the mudrā.
Thus, the characteristics of these various mudrās shall also be explained according to their respective portions.
The practitioner should reverently memorize [the ritual] and practice it until it is thoroughly mastered,
so that no error occurs during the performance of the rite.
If even the slightest doubt or mistake arises, the mudrā will not be accomplished.
If the mudrās are not correctly formed, the noble ones will not be pleased;
whatever one prays for will not achieve accomplishment.
*The Sūtra of the Ritual for Accomplishing the Great Vidyā of Bodhisattva Cundā from the Yoga Mahātantra of the Vidyādharapiṭaka*, translated by the Buddha, Fascicle Two.
The Sūtra on the Ritual for Accomplishing the Great Vidyā of Bodhisattva Cundā from the Yoga of the Vidyādharapiṭaka, Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Three. Part Three:
On the Construction of the Paṭa Image. Part Three: On the Construction of the Paṭa Image.

Nāgārjuna Bodhisattva extracted this from the Vidyādharapiṭaka. Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Imperial Censor, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, Great Master of Illuminating Teaching, the Subject Faxian, by imperial decree. At that time, the Buddha said:
I have now briefly completed the explanation of all the mudrās in this Great Yoga Teaching of the Tathāgata Mahāvairocana.
I shall now further proclaim the ritual for painting the images.
If there are practitioners who, within the Cundā rites,
cultivate the path seeking accomplishment,
they must likewise first thoroughly understand the sequential procedures for the ritual of painting the image.
If a practitioner wishes to paint an image,
they must first use a high-quality, pure, plain silk cloth.
This cloth must be free of any hair, fibers, or other impurities.
If one purchases from another,
one should give the price requested;
one must not dispute whether it is too much or too little.
Once it has been obtained,
one must first place it within a heap of rice grains for seven days and nights;
thereafter, it should be soaked in water purified with the five medicinal herbs for three days.
Alternatively, it is best to do so every five or seven days;
immediately thereafter, wash it out using pure water,
and then soak it in scented water for one full day and night.
He removed it.
Then he purified it by sprinkling it with the five kinds of pure water,
and further washed it with water infused with the five precious gems.
Only then may one mount the scroll.
Once it has been properly arranged,
the practitioner personally performs the *namo* (homage) as follows:
Homage to the seventy-seven koṭis of perfectly awakened Buddhas.
Furthermore, one should cause the painter to first purify himself;
when the time comes, having together performed this taking of refuge, [one proceeds].
Only then shall one begin to paint the various worthies and sages.
Regarding the banner (*paṭa*),
the practitioner first recites the Great Mantra to empower it.
Then, mix white clay with powder and apply it to the cloth.
Once applied, place it in a clean location;
thereafter, continue until the painting is completed.
One should always make offerings of incense, flowers,
and arghya water. If one acts according to the ritual in this manner,
it is the most superior grade.
When first beginning the work and planning the layout of the boundary lines,
they must all proceed clockwise.
First, one should paint a lotus pond on the lower part of the scroll.
It was filled with lotus flowers,
as well as various kinds of aquatic creatures such as fish, conches, clams, and turtles,
along with mandarin ducks and other flying birds.
Then, upon the surface of the pond, one should paint three lotus seats composed of various jewels;
in the center of these, upon the central lotus, [one should place the deity].
Paint the World-Honored One, the White Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa,
with flames of light pervading everywhere, blazing and radiating brilliantly;
his right hand forms the mudrā of granting boons (*varada-mudrā*).
The left hand forms the mudrā of preaching the Dharma.
The halo is white in color,
and from the center of the navel wheel, a great radiance issues forth.
Within that light appears the Bodhisattva Cunda;
on a lotus to the right of the Buddha,
one should paint the third Uṣṇīṣa.
He has six arms; the first right hand performs the gesture of granting boons (*varada-mudrā*),
the second holds a lotus flower,
and the third holds a rosary (*akṣamālā*).
The first left hand holds a vajra;
the second hand holds a scripture;
the third hand forms the mudrā of preaching the Dharma.
The body is completely surrounded by a blazing, radiant light.
On a lotus to the left, paint Amoghapāśa.
He has four faces and eight arms;
he wears a tiger skin as a garment and uses it as a sash across his chest,
and further, he wears a deer skin as a celestial robe.
The face has three eyes, and the head is adorned with a jeweled crown; the hair-knot hangs down.
The first right hand forms the varada-mudrā (gesture of granting boons), and the second hand holds a rosary.
The third hand holds a lasso;
the fourth hand forms the mudrā of granting fearlessness.
The first left hand holds a white lotus.
The second hand holds a scripture;
the third hand forms a fist with the index finger extended upward,
forming the *kṣepaṇa-mudrā* (the threatening gesture).
The fourth hand holds a hook.
Radiant flames envelop his entire body, blazing with intense brilliance.
Below him are depicted the two nāga kings, Nanda and Upananda.
Each has seven heads and holds a Buddha-seat and a lotus stalk in its hands.
To the right, one should paint Ratnasena.
Wearing a celestial crown and adorned with various ornaments, he holds a precious jewel in his hand.
Next, paint Pūrṇabhadra,
who likewise wears a celestial crown, possesses radiant light, and is decorated with various ornaments.
Above and to the left and right,
paint five Buddha-stūpas;
within the stūpas, paint the various auspicious Tathāgatas.
First, paint the Tathāgata Samudraśrī.
Second, paint the Tathāgata Ratnaśikharaśrī.
Third, paint the Tathāgata Makuṭagarbhaśrī.
The bodies of all the Tathāgatas are golden in color;
their hands form the mudrā of granting fearlessness.
Furthermore, on both the left and right sides, draw jeweled mountains.
On the jewel mountain to the left,
paint the Bodhisattva Māmakī,
seated upon a lotus throne and holding a vajra in her hand.
Next, paint Aparājita; above him, paint the Vidyārāja Takkirāja, holding a vajra.
Furthermore, on the left side, paint the Vidyārāja Vajrāṅkuśa.
Above the Buddha Bhagavān, paint clouds on both the left and right,
manifesting the appearance of lightning.
Within the clouds, depict the various devas raining down showers of precious jewels;
further, depict the various devas in the act of offering songs and music;
and above them, depict the devas of the sun and moon.
Furthermore, let various flowers descend from the sky like rain.
Next, on the mountain of the treasure-trove to the right,
paint the most supreme holy Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva of the three realms.
Holding a lotus flower in her hand,
to her immediate right,
one should paint the Bodhisattva Ārya Tārā.
Holding a blue utpala lotus in her hand;
next, on the right side, paint the Buddha-mother Māyā,
and behind her, paint Mahāmāyūrī Vidyārājñī.
Immediately to the left and right of that,
paint dancing peacocks;
furthermore, on the upper right side.
Paint the five Tathāgatas:
first, paint the Tathāgata Dharmasāgaragatirājaśrī;
second, paint the Tathāgata Suprabhārāja.
Third, the Tathāgata Maitreyavyūhaśrī;
fourth, the Tathāgata Pradīparāja; fifth, the Tathāgata Ūrṇakośaśrī.
In this manner, each of the five Tathāgatas sits upon a lotus throne.
Next, paint a yakṣa lord;
next, paint Śakra holding a parasol.
Thus, according to the dharma, one should draw the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the various worthy sages in their proper sequence,
ensuring that they are all complete in their majestic power and sovereign mastery,
so that when the gods, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits of the world behold them, they are all brought to submission.
Once the painting of the image is thus completed,
the practitioner who recites the mantra shall perform the consecration and celebratory praise for the image upon this scroll.
The practitioner begins on either the first day or the fifteenth day of the lunar month,
seeking the empowerment of all the noble sages;
immediately thereafter, having purified oneself, one proceeds.
Wearing new, clean garments and observing the precepts of the fast for three days and nights, or one day and night,
one should either maintain a pure fast without eating, or consume only vegetables, milk, and the like.
At other times, he constantly maintains his alms bowl for eating;
furthermore, having received the eight precepts,
he prepares various kinds of incense, flowers, unguents, and pure water.
Furthermore, relight the ghee lamps and use various kinds of exquisite garments, ornaments, and precious decorations for adornment.
Additionally, use five *argha* vases filled with excellent fragrant water,
as well as water containing the five jewels and the five medicinal herbs to serve as the *argha* offering.
Having made various offerings such as food and drink,
the practitioner shall then set up the painting and place it in the location where they intend to perform the recitation.
Then, with the aforementioned articles of offering,
one makes offerings to the painted scroll image.
Having thus performed the ritual for the installation of the image:
Thereafter, the practitioner should proceed according to convenience and practice in accordance with the dharma.
Furthermore, the method for painting an image of the Bodhisattva Cunda is explained:
specifically, if a practitioner wishes to paint an image of the Honored One, the Bodhisattva Cunda, they should recite [the mantra].
First, one should seek out new cloth that is pure and white.
Once the cloth has been obtained,
one should immediately have the painter prepare in advance by cleansing himself thoroughly.
On the first day of the commencement, have them receive the eight precepts.
Thereafter, have them prepare excellent pigments using new vessels and paint the Bodhisattva Cundā.
His body is like the color of the autumn moon and his face has three eyes.
He possesses eighteen arms and wears white garments, adorned with various ornaments.
He wore *aṃśuka* as his celestial robe;
he had bracelets made of *śaṅkha* jewels,
and his ten fingers were adorned with jeweled rings.
The two upper hands form the *dharmacakra-mudrā*.
The second right hand forms the *abhaya-mudrā*,
and the third hand holds a sword.
The fourth hand holds a precious bell;
the fifth hand holds a vijapura fruit;
the sixth hand holds a battle-axe.
The seventh hand holds a hook;
the eighth hand holds a vajra;
the ninth hand holds a rosary.
The second left hand holds a wish-fulfilling jewel banner;
the third hand holds a lotus flower;
and the fourth hand holds a water flask (*kamaṇḍalu*).
The fifth hand holds a noose;
the sixth hand holds a wheel;
the seventh hand holds a conch shell.
The eighth hand holds a precious vase (*bhadraghaṭa*);
the ninth hand holds the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Below the Bodhisattva, paint a lotus pond.
Within that pond, a great lotus flower has emerged,
upon which are depicted the two nāga kings, Nanda and Upananda,
holding the stalks of the lotuses.
Upon the flower, paint the Bodhisattva Cundā,
with a great circular halo blazing and filling all space.
In front of the Bodhisattva, paint the practitioner who performs the recitation.
Holding an incense burner in his hand, he assumes the posture of gazing up at the Honored One.
Above him, one should paint a deity from the Śuddhāvāsa heavens,
depicted in the act of raining down flowers and jewels.
Thus, for such a painted image, purity and single-minded devotion are paramount.
For one who performs the ritual before this image, there is nothing that will not be accomplished.

Section Four: The Ritual Manual for the Accomplishment of the Great Mantra of Bodhisattva Kuntī, concerning the Method for Constructing the Maṇḍala. Furthermore, regarding the practice of the Kuntī rite, the practitioner...
Regarding the one who practices and achieves the construction of the maṇḍala:
having first selected an excellent site according to the ritual rules,
one should immediately excavate and remove the inferior earth, sand, gravel, ash, and charcoal.
As for the hair, body hair, bones, and so forth,
fill them in separately with fine earth, compacting it until solid and making the surface perfectly level and even.
Thereafter, one should demarcate the upper portion to construct the maṇḍala.
That maṇḍala may be sixteen cubits, eight cubits, or four cubits;
these three dimensions are not fixed.
Whatever is created, whether large or small, must be strictly adorned.
The maṇḍala has four gates opening on its four sides,
and within each gate, a dharma-wheel is installed.
Within that space, use threads of five colors to mark out the lines and construct the inner maṇḍala,
arranging the positions for the eight holy deities.
The powder used to fashion the images of the worthy sages and saints should consist of five-colored precious dust;
if these are lacking, one should substitute them with five-colored powders.
Within this maṇḍala,
there are thirty-three koṭis of devas;
argha vases are distributed upon the maṇḍala.
Within each individual argha vessel,
visualize one koṭi of deities;
furthermore, within the gates of the maṇḍala.
Having settled the eight great nāga kings,
one should paint the Bodhisattva Cundā within the inner maṇḍala.
The various other worthy sages (āryas) are arranged in sequence.
In the northeast, one installs the Great Wheel Vidyārāja;
in the southeast, the Acala Vidyārāja; and in the south, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi.
In the north, place the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara;
in the northwest, place the Bodhisattva Amoghapāśa;
and in the west, place the Bodhisattva Ekajaṭā.
In the southwest, one should place the Bodhisattva Vajranakhi.
On the eastern side of the maṇḍala, one should place the aforementioned painted image on a banner.
Furthermore, on the ground in front of the banner, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus flower.
Above, one constructs a homa hearth;
therein, the practitioner performs the homa according to the ritual rules.
The practitioner first scatters rice blossoms over it all around.
Then, he sprinkles it with water containing the five medicinal herbs to purify it.
Thereafter, he establishes the outer offerings to make offerings to the worthy sages.
One should make offerings to the worthy ones and the sages using incense, flowers, unguents, conch shells,
garments, banners, streamers, and so forth, up to the *argha* vases and various other ritual implements.
Furthermore, one should offer water containing the five precious gems to the respective family (*kula*).
Having purified oneself,
one should then partake of the "three white foods," namely,
food prepared by blending ghee, milk, and curd.
Food is also categorized into three grades:
if one performs a superior rite, one should use superior offerings;
if one performs a middling rite, one should use middling offerings.
The third category of ritual application requires the third offering.
Although it is said that all three categories must consist of superior flavors,
they are used to be offered to the noble deities within the maṇḍala.
If there are any mātṛs, rākṣasas, bhūtas, or piśācas present in this assembly who have come from the ten directions in response to the invocation,
one must impartially provide them with sacrificial offerings.
Do not allow them to be deficient in anything.
The offering vessels and utensils used are also each distinct.
If one is making offerings to the eight Tathāgatas within the maṇḍala, as well as Cundā and the others, [the vessels should be prepared accordingly].
Each person first offers a single golden lotus flower the size of a thumb. Then,
having filled a copper bowl with curd, honey, and various foods,
they present it to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
However, one should use new earthenware vessels to hold the sacrificial food for those who have come from the ten directions, such as Śeṣa and others.
As for this sacrificial food, it consists of wine, meat, and fish;
alternatively, one may use whole fish as the offering.
When making offerings to the noble ones (*ārya*) and the *Viśvedevas* and others, one must maintain focused body and mind and perform the worship with utmost devotion.
When the noble ones are thus pleased, whatever is sought will be accomplished. Having performed it in this manner:
The practitioner then enters into meditative visualization.
They should imagine that there is an object upon the tip of their own nose;
once this has become manifest before them, [they should proceed].
By focusing the mind without distraction, one achieves steadfast loving-kindness;
this causes the inhalation and exhalation to become subtle.
Sitting upright with the head slightly bowed, one reflects that this is sufficient for oneself.
One should then visualize a sun disk appearing within the heart;
within that sun disk, one visualizes a fully blossomed lotus flower made of various jewels, and within that lotus flower, the Bodhisattva Cundā.
His body is golden in color, clad in pure white garments, and adorned with various ornaments.
One should further imagine that great radiance issues forth from the five parts of the Bodhisattva’s body,
and further imagine that light also issues forth from his nine apertures.
That light blazes intensely, illuminating all things.
Once the visualization is completed, withdraw the light and arise.
Then, offer incense, flowers, arghya water, and so forth.
Having presented these to the noble ones and sages, one pays them homage with reverence.
Furthermore, the practitioner should paint images and construct maṇḍalas,
arranging the positions of the noble ones and performing various rites.
All must receive the instructions of the ācārya and not disobey them in the slightest.
One must memorize this ritual manual in its entirety so that no error or deviation occurs.
The disciple then followed the instructions to arrange the worthy and holy ones according to the ritual protocol.
Having prepared incense, flowers, and various other requisites,
he made offerings to the worthy and holy ones.
The ācārya covers the disciple’s face with silk and instructs the disciple to hold a flower and toss it onto the maṇḍala;
the disciple shall identify the deity’s image upon which the flower lands.
May [the deity] forever be the protector of one's own person.
Hereafter, constantly recite this root mantra of the noble being (*ārya*) to seek their protection.
Having thus cast the flower and identified the tutelary deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), [proceed].
The disciple then filled a bowl with five kinds of jewels and presented it to the ācārya as an offering of gratitude for his labor.
Thus did the disciple [behave] toward the ācārya.
From then on, he honored him a thousand times more than his father;
even using the offerings made in the maṇḍala and all manner of precious gems,
he bestowed them upon all śramaṇas.
From this point forward, one should always show respect and honor toward virtuous persons and all elders;
furthermore, one must not [misappropriate] any of the articles used for the maṇḍala.
One must not even show contempt for fire, ghee, curd, and so forth,
nor may one step upon lotus flowers.
Having thus instructed and cautioned the disciple, the ācārya—
The disciple prostrated in thanks.
Thereafter, whatever rites the disciple desired to perform,
he practiced according to the ritual manual and achieved success without exception.

5. The Section on the Homa Ritual, Part Five. Furthermore, if a practitioner wishes to practice the Cundā homa ritual, they should [direct their devotion] toward the Bodhisattva Cundā and the worthy sages of the maṇḍala.
Perform a great offering.
First, prepare *jāti* flowers, *mālī* flowers,
and various other named flowers, along with exquisite incenses and the like.
Having performed the offerings,
one should then carry out the homa according to the ritual as desired.
If this practitioner wishes to attain all the accomplishments sought, [they must proceed accordingly].
First, burn wood from auspicious trees within the homa fire-pit.
Then, further use white sandalwood, camphor, and other exquisite incenses;
mix these with clarified butter and milk, and dip them in blue lotuses.
One who performs homa while reciting the Great Mantra (mahāvidyā) shall immediately obtain their wishes.
The Great Mantra is as follows:
Namo sabhdatānām samyak-sambuddha-koṭīnām oṃ cale cule cuṇḍe. If for the purpose of pacifying misfortunes (śānti).
If one uses leaves of the amra tree, smeared with ghee and milk,
and performs homa by burning them together,
one will immediately obtain their wishes.
If one wishes to perform an rite for increase (puṣṭi),
one should use aśvattha wood, or palāśa wood, or udumbara wood;
such woods as these should be used as fuel.
If one performs homa by burning ghee, honey, and curd together,
one will immediately obtain their wishes.
The great mantra is as follows:
Oṃ cale cule cuṇḍe oṃ phaṭ. If one intends to dispatch the *setuḥ* (the fetter), [recite this].
Use wood from an inauspicious tree as fuel;
soak it in oil and kindle a fire.
Furthermore, employ one ayuta of gṛdhrapāda-śrīkhaṇḍa.
For one who recites the Great Mantra (mahāvidyā) while performing homa, they shall immediately obtain their wish.
The mantra is as follows: HŪṂ PHAṬ JALE JRALE PHAṬ SVĀHĀ HŪṂ PHAṬ. If one intends to destroy a *śatru* (enemy) or to restrain their mind, [this mantra should be used].
Burn *jātī* wood as fuel for the fire.
Mix blood with mustard oil and use leaves from the *nimba* tree and thorns from the *vilva* tree.
Recite one *ayuta* of the aforementioned Great Mantra for dispatching;
by performing the *homa*, one will immediately attain all wishes.
Furthermore, for one who desires all accomplishments,
it is first necessary to receive empowerment;
thereafter, one must generate a firm resolve.
If one constantly maintains the practice of Bodhisattva Cunda, all who subsequently perform the ritual methods will attain accomplishment.
Section Six: The Ritual Method for Reciting the Dharani of Bodhisattva Cunda, Part Seven. Furthermore, if a practitioner wishes to cultivate the recitation within the ritual method of Cunda:
One must first receive the samaya and bind the maṇḍala before one may begin the recitation.
While performing the recitation:
At dawn each day, the practitioner first empowers their thumb seven times with the Great Mantra of the Great Powerful Vidyārāja.
Having protected the body,
one should also go to the place of excrement or urine; having empowered the crown of the head, the two arms, the heart, and the throat— these five locations—
one then enters into contact.
The Great Mantra of the Greatly Powerful Vidyārāja is as follows:
*Ratnavajra-nati oṃ krodhana hūṃ jaḥ*. Having recited it, one should purify the ground and the *gomaya* (cow dung) with this mantra.
Furthermore, recite the Great Mantra of Amṛtakuṇḍalī seven times to consecrate the earth,
then wash the body— including the area below the navel—
and use it to wash the lower garment.
Furthermore, one must wash one's hands again to attain purity.
Taking earth, recite the Great Mantra:
Oṃ nikhaṇa vasudhā svāhā. Having taken the earth, [proceed].
Place it in a clean location or use it for purification; that is,
take a small amount of earth and wash your hands and feet with it.
Then, recite the Great Mantra for Purification:
*Namo samantabuddhānām | oṃ jvatiṣṭhusadane svāhā*. Having recited this mantra of purification, [proceed].
Forming a fist with the thumbs extended upward, one recites the Great Vidyā of Amṛtakuṇḍalī to consecrate the five places of the body.
The Great Vidyā of Amṛtakuṇḍalī is as follows:
Namo ratnatrayāya. Namo śrīmanmahākrodhāya. Oṃ hulu hulu tiṣṭha tiṣṭha bandha bandha hana hana amṛte hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. Having recited this mantra, [one should proceed].
Furthermore, recite the Great Mantra of Samādhi three or seven times.
The Great Mantra of Samādhi is as follows:

*Namaḥ sarvabuddhabodhisattvānām | avirañje avirañje mahāvajriśānte śānte śāradate śāradate trāye trāye vidhamani sambharani haramate siddhagiri traṭ svāhā*. Having recited this mantra, take one cupful of water.
Having empowered [the water] with the aforementioned Great Mantra of Amṛtakuṇḍalī,
when sprinkling it upon one’s own crown and purifying one’s hands,
one should further recite the Great Mantra of the respective family seven times.
The Great Illumination says:
"Oṃ hūḥ. Having recited this mantra to perform the purification, one again forms a fist and places the thumb at the heart.
Recite the heart-mantra:
Oṃ bhrūṃ phaṭ. Having recited the heart-mantra once, recite the armor-mantra again.
To protect one's own five places, the mantra for the armor is:
Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ vajrapaṃjara hūṃ phaṭ. Having recited this mantra, [one should perform the protection].
Again, recite the great vidyā-mantra of Amṛtakuṇḍalī to consecrate the water;
sprinkle seven handfuls for purification and to dispel obstructing māras.
Again, recite the earth-armour vidyā-mantra.
One should empower five places of the body as armor.
This is no different from being personally protected by the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi himself.
The mantra for the earth armor is as follows:
Namo samantabuddhānām | Oṃ bhūrikara hūṃ | Having recited this mantra, [one should proceed].
Furthermore, recite the heart-mantra of the Tathāgata family to consecrate the water.
Offer three handfuls to the Three Jewels.
The great heart-mantra of the Tathāgata family is as follows:
Namo samanta-buddhānāṃ jaṃ jaḥ kum. Having recited this vidyā, one should again recite the great vidyā of Buddhalocanā to consecrate the water.
Take three handfuls of water and pour them over the crown of one’s head.
The Great Vidyā of Buddhalocanā is:
*Namaḥ sarvatathāgatebhyo viśuddhe oṃ ruru sphuru jvala tiṣṭha siddhalocane sarvārthasādhani svāhā*. Then, recite the heart-mantra of Amṛtakuṇḍalī to consecrate the water.
Take three handfuls and use them for the consecration;
this immediately constitutes the mental bath.

Oṃ amṛte hūṃ. Recite the aforementioned purification mantra again.

Within the maṇḍala, nine positions are to be arranged according to the sequential method.

Such subtle and wondrous syllables are present within all great mantras (*mahāvidyā*).

The syllable *Sva* can protect oneself and destroy enemies;

Furthermore, regarding the various mantras,
there are specific methods for accomplishment according to the syllables added:
if the syllable *oṃ* is added, it serves to awaken [the deity] and to perform the dismissal.
If the three syllables Oṃ Le Hūṃ are added, its power is able to sever and cut.
If the five syllables Oṃ Ra Hūṃ Phaṭ are added,
its power is able to terrify, destroy, and also provide protection.
If the four syllables Oṃ juna namaḥ are added,
one can accomplish the rite of magnetizing.
If the three syllables Oṃ juṃ hūṃ are added, [the same applies].
If one adds the four syllables *oṃ le phaṭ*, it can repel enemy armies and pacify great battles;
if one performs the rite for averting calamities (*śāntika*), it shall bring peace.

This Great Tārā teaching, as expounded by all the Buddhas,
